steps.text:
This position, with knights on c6 and f6, is the one place in your London where you stop and think. It has come up 245 times by two move orders, and you have tried five different fourth moves, at nearly four seconds each.

Your results do not depend on the choice: Nf3 has scored 49% (134 games) and c4 51% (88 games). So this lesson is not fixing a bad move. It is about having one answer, so the clock stays with you.

What Black is up to. The knight on c6 blocks Black's own c-pawn, so the usual ...c5 is off the table. Instead Black has two quick ideas: the bishop to f5 and the knight to b4, both aimed at c2; or ...e5 in one go.

One move for every order: c4. You already play it when the bishop comes to f5 first, so nothing new to learn. It hits d5 while the c6 knight is in the way of ...c6, and it opens a4 and b3 for your queen.Nf3 is just as good. Pick one and stop choosing.
Thing one: ...Nb4 is a mistake, and Qa4+ punishes it. The knight has left c6, so the check cannot be blocked comfortably and the knight on b4 is hanging at the end of it.

If the knight goes home with Nc6, then cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3. Your knight comes out with tempo on the queen, the knight on c6 is still pinned, and Nb5 hitting c7 is next. Black has moved the same knight three times and is losing material.
Thing two: ...e5 is answered with the bishop. Bxe5, and after Nxe5 dxe5 you are simply a pawn up. Taking with the d-pawn instead hands Black the initiative for the pawn.

Thing three: the pin on c3. After e6 Nc3 Bb4 you have played Qb3 in 17 of 31 games and scored 35% with it. It looks active and wins nothing, and the engine puts it about two-thirds of a pawn behind plain development.

Nf3, then Rc1 and the bishop out. If you want the centre settled first, cxd5 is fine too. These moves are interchangeable.The rule that covers all of it: in the ...Nc6 lines the queen goes to a4 with check when the knight jumps to b4, and otherwise stays home until you have castled. Qb3 is not your move while a knight can hit it from b4 or a5.

cards.t: London: when the knight comes to c6

steps.text:
You have played the Englund 682 times in these games and scored 50%. The engine thinks it costs Black about a pawn from move one, and nothing in this lesson changes that. Whether to keep it is a separate decision.

What this lesson does is narrower. A handful of positions come up again and again, and in each you tend to play the same second-best move. Those are cheap to fix.

They decline with Nf3. You have answered Nc6 in 26 of 34 games. It runs into d5 and the knight gets kicked around.e4 instead. The pawn gains time on the knight and you are already comfortable. (exd4 is also fine.)

They push past with d5. You nearly always play f5 (64 of 70). The engine prefers plain development by about four-fifths of a pawn: Bc5, then ...d6 and ...Nf6. The pawn on d5 has given you the c5 square for free, so use it.
They play c3, e3 or c4 instead of taking. Just take: exd4. You get a normal position with equal chances and no gambit to justify.

The main line. dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7. Now it depends on White's fourth move.

Against e3 you have played Qb4+ in 7 of 37 games, and it is an error every time. There is no bishop on d2 to trap and no pawn on b2 worth the time: White just develops with tempo. Take the pawn back, Nxe5.
Against Qd5 the check is wrong again. f6 is the move: it breaks up the e5 pawn and gets your pieces out.
The line the opening is played for. Bf4 Qb4+ Bd2 Qxb2. If White now defends with Bc3, the bishop move you know: Bb4.
Qd2 loses on the spot to Bxc3 Qxc3 Qc1 mate.

But when White takes, Bxb4, recapture with the knight. Nxb4 threatens both the rook on a1 and a fork on c2, and White cannot cover both.

In your games you took the rook at once with Qxa1 every time. That is still good for you, but after Bd2 the queen is short of squares and most of the advantage is gone.
White plays it properly: Nc3. Now Bb4 Rb1 Qa3, and you are at the position where your clock use triples. There are three White moves and one answer to each.
Rb3: the queen has exactly one square. Qa5.
Nb5: take the bishop with check first, Bxd2+, and only then Qxa2. Taking on a2 at once runs into Rxb4, and after the recapture Nxc7+ forks king and rook.

Nd5: the refutation you know from the White side. Bxd2+ Qxd2 Kd8 is the best there is. You are worse here, by about two pawns in the engine's view, and there is no trick that fixes it. This is the real price of the opening against someone who knows it.

The other knight jump: Nd5 a move earlier, before Rb1. Bxd2+ Nxd2, and now c7 is hit. You have played Qxe5 here every time. It walks into Nc4, which hits the queen and renews the threat on c7.Kd8 covers c7 first. The e5 pawn will still be there next move.
One more. When White plays Nc3 on move three, before Nf3, do not play Qe7 out of habit: Nd5 hits the queen and c7 at once. Take the pawn, Nxe5.

cards.t: Englund: the spots where your games repeat

steps.text: You have said the Caro feels less understood than the London: the moves are known, the plans are not. The short version is that the pawn structure tells you the plan, and the Advance and the Exchange are two different structures with two different jobs.

The Advance. White's pawns on d4 and e5 form a chain pointing at your kingside. A chain is attacked at its base, and the base is d4. Everything you do in this line is about d4.

Your move c5 hits it first. Nc6 hits it second.
Bg4. Two reasons, both about d4. The bishop gets outside your pawns before ...e6 shuts the door. And it pins, or trades itself for, the f3 knight, which is d4's main defender.

Then e6, the knight from g8 to e7 and on to f5, and the queen to b6. That is three attackers on one pawn, with the bishop tying down its defender. Which of ...Nge7 and ...Qb6 comes first does not matter.

This is the position to carry in your head: every piece has a job and the job is d4.

Your one repeat error here. When White plays h3, you have retreated to h5 in 4 of 8 games. Then g4 and e6 follow, and White has the initiative.

Take the knight. Bxf3. If the queen recaptures, Nxd4 wins the base of the chain. If the pawn recaptures, White's kingside is wrecked. This is what the bishop went to g4 for.

The Exchange. No chain, no base, no target on d4. The pawns are symmetrical except for one thing: you have a half-open c-file and White has a half-open e-file.

So the job changes. First, develop without getting the bishop stuck: knights to c6 and f6, bishop out to g4 or f5, and only then ...e6.
The one move to know: Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together. Qd7 covers both. (Qc8 and Na5 are equally good. It does not matter which.)

Then ...e6, ...Bd6, castle. In the middlegame your plan is on the queenside: rooks to the c-file and b-file, and the b-pawn up to b4 to make c3 a target. It is called the minority attack. White's play is on the kingside and the e-file.

Advance: hit d4. Exchange: c-file and the b-pawn.

The Panov, c4. A third structure: White is going to end up with an isolated pawn on d4, and until then has pressure on d5. Here the order of your moves matters.

After Nc6 Nc3 you have played Bf5 in 5 of 8 games. It loses about a piece's worth: cxd5 hits the knight, which has no good square, and d5 is gone.

In the Panov the knights come first and the bishop stays home until d5 is secure. Nf6, then e6, then the bishop to e7 or b4.

When White finally takes on d5 you recapture with a piece, and you have what you want: a knight sitting on d5 in front of an isolated pawn. From there, trade minor pieces. The fewer pieces left, the weaker that pawn gets.

steps.text:
Worth fixing: the knight on g5. After Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Nf6, some opponents dodge the trade with Ng5. You have met it 29 times and scored 31%, and you have tried seven different replies.

The knight is aiming at f7 with a bishop coming to c4. Do not let it settle.

h6. Ask the question at once. The knight has to retreat, and its trip has gained nothing. Then develop normally: ...Bf5 or ...Bg4, ...e6.

With the sample this small the 31% could be luck. But one reply is still better than seven.

Not worth fixing: a5 against the bishop on b3. After Bc4 d5 exd5 cxd5 Bb3 you play a5 nearly every time (86 of 98). The engine likes plain development about a third of a pawn more.

You score 51% from here, and a third of a pawn in the opening is inside the noise at any level you will play at. Keep it if you like it. It is a move that does not matter.

Against 1.e4 and 1.d4 your first moves are automatic. Against everything else there is no settled reply at all: about 70 games a year start with you thinking on move one.

Mostly the results are fine. Against b3 your ...e5 has scored 78% (18 games), against e3 62% (17). The exception is c4: 56 games, and 41% with ...e5. That is a small sample and could be chance, but it is also the one of these where ...e5 leads to positions you have never studied.
Rule one: if they let you, take the centre. Against b3 and e3, keep doing what works: e5, then ...d5 or ...Nc6, and develop. Nothing to learn.
Rule two: against c4, play your Caro pawns. c6, then d5. You already know what these pawns do.
If White plays e4, you are in a Caro-Kann. After d5 exd5 cxd5 d4 it is the Panov from the Caro lesson: knights first.
If White takes twice instead, cxd5, do not rush to take back with the queen. Nf6 first, and the pawn on d5 falls anyway.

If White keeps it quiet with Nf3 and g3, set up the London with colours reversed: pawns on c6, d5 and e6, bishop outside them first. Here Bg4 is a shade better than f5, because a queen on b3 then has less to hit.

If White plays d4, it is a Slav. One thing to know. When White has knights on both c3 and f3, the bishop does not come out: Bf5 runs into cxd5 and Qb3, hitting b7 and d5. It is the same trick you use yourself in the London.

Play e6 instead and develop behind the pawns: ...Nbd7, ...Bd6, castle.

Rule three: g3, f4 and the rest. d5 on move one, then the same set-up: ...c6 if the d-pawn needs support, bishop out to f5 or g4, ...e6, ...Nf6. Against 1.Nf3 you already play ...d5 and score well. Leave that alone.

None of this needs memorising past move three. The point is that move one stops costing time.
